name: Battle of Magnesia
info: Roman and Pergamene forces under the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and Eumenes II defeated the Seleucid army of Antiochus III near Magnesia ad Sipylum in Asia Minor, which led to the Treaty of Apamea.

facts.place: A plain north-east of Magnesia ad Sipylum, between the rivers Phrygios and Hermos, in Asia Minor (modern Manisa, Turkey)
facts.sides: The Roman Republic under the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and the Kingdom of Pergamon under Eumenes II, about 30,000 men according to Livy and Appian, perhaps 50,000 by some modern historians; the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus III, about 72,000 according to Livy and Appian, perhaps 50,000 by some modern historians
facts.outcome: A Roman and Pergamene victory. The Seleucid army broke and fled, cities surrendered to the Romans, and the Treaty of Apamea ended Seleucid domination in Asia Minor.

t: Livy and Appian agree on about 30,000 Romans and 72,000 Seleucids, but some modern historians think each army may have had about 50,000 men.
Eumenes broke the Seleucid left with missile troops and a cavalry charge, while the Seleucid phalanx fell apart when its elephants panicked under a hail of projectiles.
By the Treaty of Apamea Antiochus gave up his claims west of the Taurus Mountains, and most of Asia Minor west of the Taurus went to the Attalids of Pergamon.
dyk: Livy gives 53,000 Seleucid dead against 349 Romans, while modern estimates give 10,000 Seleucids and 5,000 Romans killed.
ev: Antiochus meets Roman envoys at Lysimachia, who demand that he leave Europe and restore the autonomy of the Greek cities of Asia Minor
Antiochus lands in Greece at Demetrias at the urging of the Aetolians, and Rome declares war in November
The Romans defeat Antiochus at Thermopylae and, in September, his fleet at Corycus
A combined Roman and Rhodian fleet defeats the Seleucid fleet at Myonessus, opening the way to Asia Minor
Scipio and Eumenes defeat Antiochus at Magnesia ad Sipylum
A truce is signed at Sardes
The Romans begin the Galatian War, and peace talks are held with the Senate
The Treaty of Apamea is signed

sections.background:
After campaigns in Bactria and India, Antiochus III allied with Philip V of Macedon and won the Fifth Syrian War in 198 BCE, taking Coele-Syria. He then turned to Asia Minor. In 196 BCE he used the death of Attalus I to attack cities held by the Attalid dynasty, and his troops crossed the Hellespont to rebuild Lysimachia. Smyrna and Lampsacus, fearing that he would take all of Asia Minor, appealed to Rome for protection.

At Lysimachia in October 196 BCE the Romans demanded that Antiochus withdraw from Europe and restore the autonomy of the Greek city-states of Asia Minor. He answered that he was rebuilding the empire of his ancestor Antiochus II Theos and criticised Roman meddling in states whose rights Rhodes had traditionally defended. Hannibal fled to Antiochus' court at Ephesus in the winter of 196 and 195 BCE. The Aetolian League promised Antiochus its support in 193 BCE and then seized Demetrias, and in September 192 BCE the Aetolian general Thoantas persuaded him to oppose the Romans openly in Greece.

The war went against Antiochus. He was defeated at Thermopylae in April 191 BCE, his fleet lost at Corycus and Myonessus, and he lost control of the Aegean. He offered to pay half the Roman war expenses and to accept the demands made at Lysimachia, but the Romans were by then determined to crush the Seleucids once and for all.
sections.forces:
Livy and Appian both give the Roman army as about 30,000 men and the Seleucid army as approximately 72,000. Modern historians disagree: some accept the figures of the primary sources, while others hold that each army may have numbered some 50,000. The Romans had 16 African war elephants, considered inferior to the Asian elephants of the Seleucids, who had 54. The Romans were led by the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and were joined by the army of Eumenes II of Pergamon.

Antiochus' left wing was commanded by his son Seleucus and his nephew Antipater, and he led the right himself. The centre was a Macedonian phalanx of 16,000 under Philip, the master of the elephants, drawn up in ten taxeis, each 50 men wide and 32 deep, with elephants in pairs in the gaps. Ahead of the left flank stood scythed chariots and camel-borne Arab archers, with 6,000 light infantry beside them. Seven thousand of the least combat-ready troops guarded the camp.

On the Roman side the legate Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus held the left with 10,800 heavy infantry, and Scipio the centre with another 10,800 in three lines, in a more open and flexible formation than their adversaries. Eumenes held the right with 2,800 to 3,000 cavalry, mostly Roman, with an 800-man Pergamene force. Light infantry and archers stood ahead of the main force, and 2,000 Thracian and Macedonian volunteers with the elephants formed the rearguard.
sections.course:
The Romans marched from Pergamon towards Thyatira, but Antiochus camped 15 kilometres north-east of Magnesia ad Sipylum, and the Romans camped 6.5 kilometres from him, north of the Hermos. They refused to be lured out by a detachment of 1,000 Galatian and Dahae cavalry, then moved to a horseshoe-shaped plain about 4 kilometres from the Seleucid camp, enclosed on three sides by the Phrygios and the Hermos. For five days the armies lined up without fighting. Scipio could not storm a fortified camp and wished to win before a new consul replaced him. The Romans advanced to where the Phrygios turned north, leaving their right flank unprotected, and Antiochus accepted battle at dawn on the third day after.

Eumenes sent archers, slingers and spearmen against the scythed chariots, which fled in panic and threw the camel archers and cataphracts behind them into confusion. He then charged with his cavalry before the cataphracts could reorganise, broke through the Seleucid left and drove them to the camp.

On the other wing Antiochus attacked with his cataphracts and agema cavalry and the argyraspides, and the Roman infantry broke and fell back to their camp, where they were reinforced and rallied by the tribune Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. Antiochus' cavalry became bogged down at the camp. The phalanx held but could not dislodge the archers and slingers bombarding it. As it began a slow, organised retreat its elephants panicked and broke its formation. The phalangites discarded their weapons and left the field, and Antiochus' army had dispersed before his cavalry returned.
sections.aftermath:
According to Livy, 53,000 Seleucid soldiers died, 1,400 were captured and 15 elephants were taken, while the Romans lost 349 men with many more wounded. Modern estimates give 10,000 dead for the Seleucids and 5,000 killed for the Romans. Antiochus gathered the survivors and retreated to Sardes while the Romans were busy looting his camp. There he learnt that his son Seleucus had survived, and he went to Apamea to meet him.

The defeat and the withdrawal of the Seleucid fleet from Ephesus to Patara led the garrisons of Sardes, Ephesus, Thyatira and Magnesia ad Sipylum itself to surrender to the Romans. Antiochus sent Zeuxis and Antipater to seek a truce, which was signed at Sardes in January 189 BCE. He agreed to abandon his claims to all lands west of the Taurus Mountains, pay a heavy indemnity and hand over Hannibal and other notable enemies of Rome among his allies.

The Romans began the Galatian War to subjugate Asia Minor and punish Antiochus' allies, and in Greece they suppressed the Athamanians and Aetolians, who had broken the terms of an earlier truce. In the summer of 189 BCE envoys of the Seleucids, Pergamon, Rhodes and other states held peace talks with the Senate. Lycia and Caria were given to Rhodes, and the Attalids received Thrace and most of Asia Minor west of the Taurus. Antiochus also had to hand over Hannibal, Thoantas and twenty notables as hostages, keep only ten ships, and give Rome 40,500 modiuses of grain a year. The terms took effect with the Treaty of Apamea in the summer of 188 BCE.
sections.sources:
The two main historical accounts of the battle are Livy's Ab Urbe Condita Libri and Appian's Syriaca. They agree on the sizes of the armies, about 30,000 Romans and some 72,000 Seleucids, but modern historians dispute those figures, and some think each army may have numbered about 50,000. The same gap separates the casualty figures: Livy has 53,000 Seleucid dead and 349 Roman, against modern estimates of 10,000 and 5,000.

The date is also uncertain, since the battle took place either in December 190 or January 189 BCE. The story that Antiochus asked Hannibal whether his army would be enough for the Romans, and Hannibal answered that it was quite enough for the Romans, however greedy they were, is called a popular anecdote.
sections.legacy:
The battle was a decisive Roman and Pergamene victory, and it led to the Treaty of Apamea, which ended Seleucid domination in Asia Minor. Antiochus gave up his claims west of the Taurus, and the Attalids of Pergamon and Rhodes were the main gainers. Lycia and Caria went to Rhodes, and Thrace and most of Asia Minor west of the Taurus to the Attalids, while the independence of the city-states that had sided with Rome before the battle was guaranteed.

Magnesia also marked the end of the Macedonian phalanx's dominance on the battlefields of the Hellenistic period. The Seleucid phalanx held its ground against the Roman infantry, but it was not mobile enough to answer the archers and slingers, and its own elephants broke it. The battlefield itself had been used before, for the Seleucid victory at Corupedium in 281 BCE.

summary: Near Magnesia ad Sipylum, in December 190 or January 189 BCE, Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and Eumenes II of Pergamon defeated Antiochus III's army. Livy gives 53,000 Seleucid dead, modern estimates 10,000. The Treaty of Apamea ended Seleucid domination in Asia Minor.
references: John Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (Brill, 2002)
Bezalel Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army: Organization and Tactics in the Great Campaigns (Cambridge University Press, 1976)
Michael Taylor, Antiochus The Great (Pen and Sword Military, 2013)
notes: Strengths: Livy and Appian 30,000 and 72,000; some modern historians say about 50,000 each. Casualties: Livy 53,000 Seleucids dead, 1,400 captured, 349 Romans; modern estimates 10,000 and 5,000. All given with their hedges.
The article's date is 'either December 190 or January 189 BC'; ev, span and start/end follow that. The truce is dated January 189.

The article is thin on sources: it names only Livy and Appian and gives no archaeology, so the sources section is short and the legacy section rests on the treaty and the end of the phalanx's dominance.
The sentence 'Magnesia had already served as a battlefield ... Corupedium in 281 BC' is used in legacy; it is a fact about the site, not a legacy, so the editor may move or cut it.

The Seleucid wings list in the article has oddities (16 elephants on the left wing and 16 in reserve on the right, 20 in the centre; 'Atian' infantry); I gave only the totals and the centre. The article's Seleucid left wing is composed of both left and centre troops in one paragraph.
The article says Scipio was in a 'zugzwang'; I paraphrased his dilemma. 'Quite enough for the Romans' anecdote is told as an anecdote, with no attribution in the article.
The article's number of Seleucid troops raised for Greece (10,000 infantry, 500 cavalry, 6 elephants, 300 ships) is left out; Pergamon's army uniting at the Caecus is left out for length.
The 'Battle of the Eurymedon' (Rhodians beat Hannibal's fleet) is left out; the article's 'Seleucids ... 300 ships' and the Aetolians' capture of Demetrias are mentioned briefly.
